_comment: The frame fetch every channel under the Snapchat heading runs.
Named rather than repeated per channel, and that is not tidiness. A
pack under this heading is made by copying the folder next to it and
changing the brand, and every key restated in each of them is a key a
new channel can silently be missing — which is exactly what happened:
channels arrived captioning their frames with the transcript as
spoken, because the copy they were made from predated `rewrite`. One
definition means a new channel inherits the whole of this by writing
one line, and means a change to it reaches every channel at once.
_comment_frames: Forty is where the slider OPENS, and one is as low as it goes.
The opening figure is the ask these channels exist for - a set to work
through - and it stays forty because that is what somebody who does
not touch the slider should get. The floor used to be forty as well,
on the argument that a set of five is not a set; that argument is
about the usual job and not about every job, and it cost the user the
one case the slider is quickest for, which is pulling a single frame
Two hundred is the upper end, which is a long video's worth at this
spacing and well inside what the up-front edit pass can get through.
The count is not only a number of pictures. It is the rewrite's
budget: 80 characters a frame, so forty frames is an account of at
most 3,200 characters and two hundred of at most 16,000, dealt out
over the frames in order with a piece on every one. The count used is
the number of frames the run actually delivered, confirmed once they
_comment_output: 540x960 is the vertical full-screen frame these are cut for. It is the
one number both halves of the app have to agree on, and they do not
each hold a copy of it: this is where it is stated, the backend is
told it in the framing the pack sends (see channels.framingFor), and
the frontend canvas is set from it (see config.setCanvasSize).
_comment_captions: What puts words back on a frame that was originally handed over bare.
The run transcribes the video's voice track and each still comes back
with the sentence that was being said at the moment it was cut from -
the frames already knew when they happened, so all it took was the
words knowing the same thing. See backend/transcriber.py.

_comment_rewrite: The transcript is not set as spoken. It is REWRITTEN before it is set:
turned from speech into ONE third-person account of the video, read
from the first frame to the last, and dealt out over the frames in
order - every frame with a piece of it. See backend/narrator.py for
what that means and for what it refuses to do.
It exists because these videos are half narration and half interview,
and only the narration half already reads as information. An interview
is somebody talking about themselves to a reporter who is not on
screen, and a still captioned "I am Brian, Dolly's son" is a caption
of nobody. Reported instead, direct speech becomes described speech -
"I am Dolly Parton's grandson" becomes "Brian said he was Dolly
Parton's grandson" - and the same facts read as news.
Written to the frame count: 80 characters a frame. A sentence takes one
frame, or two when it needs up to 160 characters; a thought that needs
more than that is cut there and carried on in the next sentence.
Names are varied as the account goes - the full name first, then a
pronoun, a role, the surname, the first name - see
backend/reference.py.
It does not translate. The caption is the video's own words over the
video's own pictures, so a Portuguese interview reported in English
captions something nobody said - and that is the one failure here that
does not LOOK like one, since it reads perfectly. Asking for "the same
language as the transcript" was measured and failed on every line of a
Portuguese transcript and every line of a French one. The language is
NAMED instead, from what Whisper detected on its way to the words, and
a second check drops any line that still reads as English on a video
that was not.
One line per thought, not per transcript sentence. A speaker
introducing themselves and then saying what they came to say is three
sentences and one piece of news, so the three are gathered into one
item before the model sees them. It is never asked WHERE a line
should begin - offered a syntax for joining lines itself, it used it
zero times in sixty-three sentences, and zero times again when told
joining was the expected move.
No timestamps. Only the words of the transcript go in, and nothing in
the account is matched to a moment of the video: the frames and the
transcript are both in the order the video runs, so the first piece
of the account goes on the first frame and the rest follow.
Read once as the run starts, in the same breath as `captions`, the
frame count and the output size. It cannot be a per-frame answer for
the reason none of those can: it decides what the RUN produces, and by
the time there is a grid to look at, the words on it have already been
chosen.
It needs `captions` to mean anything, a rewrite of a transcription
nobody asked for being nothing at all. Set without it, the backend
ignores it - there is no transcript to rewrite.
Nothing about it is fatal, which is the rule every model in this app
is held to. A machine that has never fetched the weights, or a model
that produces nothing usable for the whole video, leaves the frames
the transcript as spoken; a single line that comes back malformed
keeps its own words as spoken. Plainer, not wrong.
There is no channel under this heading that turns it off, and the two
that existed to be compared with and without it are gone. If one ever
wants the transcript as spoken it says so here, in its own pack, by
overriding this key - which is the shape every exception to a shared
guideline takes.
